The constant 0.358 gives the CHILL+ count slope again.
On the secondary prism it is 120.2, 118.0, 111.9, 88.2, 64.1 and
52.0 Å/ns from 220 K to 265 K.
The mislabel q6bar sits a few angstroms per nanosecond above the
CHILL+ slope and does not move the ordering.
The basal face is the slowest at each temperature.
From 220 K to 260 K it is 0.48 to 0.66 of the secondary prism, around
the 0.6 ratio Espinosa, Navarro, Sanz, Valeriani and Vega report for
TIP4P/ICE.
At 265 K the ratio is 0.39.
The two prisms agree from 230 K to 260 K.
At 220 K the secondary prism is faster than the primary, 119.2
against 101.2, and the intervals do not overlap.
At 265 K they do not overlap either, 50.4 against 30.0.
One primary-prism seed at 230 K is 151 Å/ns.
The other three are 84, 107 and 108, which is why that interval is
the wide one.

The curve on each face is a Wilson-Frenkel form with the melting
point fixed at the Table II value, 274.6 K,

u(T) = A exp(−B/T) \[1 − exp(−C (Tm − T)/T)\].

A, B and C are the least-squares values on the six CHILL+ means.
A large A with a small C can describe the same six means, so the
separate parameters are not a measured activation energy.
The maximum is read from the curve on a 0.05 K grid.
The interval resamples the seeds inside each temperature, refits,
and takes the 2.5 and 97.5 percentiles of 1000 maxima.

| face | T of maximum (K) | maximum (Å/ns) | highest measured mean |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| basal | 228.7 [219.2, 234.9] | 64.9 [59.7, 71.6] | 71.1 at 230 K |
| primary prism | 225.3 [217.4, 231.5] | 108.4 [98.3, 120.8] | 112.4 at 230 K |
| secondary prism | 218.1 [200.0, 226.7] | 120.0 [115.4, 128.3] | 119.2 at 220 K |

The basal and primary-prism maxima sit between the 220 K and 240 K
measurements.
The secondary-prism means at 220 K and 230 K agree, and the fitted
maximum is at 218 K.
The lower end of that interval is 200 K, the edge of the grid on
which the maximum is sought, so the turnover has not been resolved
below the coldest point that was run.
By 240 K the secondary prism has already fallen, and it keeps
falling through 265 K.

Four times the secondary-prism count slope is the factor-of-four
reading of Table I.
At 240 K that is 447 \[423, 481\], and the printed 490 lies above
the interval.
At 250 K it is 348 \[314, 385\], and the printed 375 lies inside.
At 260 K it is 253 \[232, 278\], and the printed 266 lies inside.
The ratios of the count slope to the printed column are 0.23, 0.23
and 0.24.
The ratios to the column divided by four are 0.91, 0.93 and 0.95.
Table II, ln(u/(Å/ns)) = 4.1711 + 0.096266 ΔT − 0.001148 (ΔT)^2,
peaks at 232.7 K.
The printed peak is 487 Å/ns and the factor-of-four reading is
121.9 Å/ns, next to the 120 Å/ns secondary-prism maximum here, at a
warmer temperature.
Dividing the Table II curve by four gives 101, 121, 115, 86, 52 and
37 Å/ns at 220, 230, 240, 250, 260 and 265 K.
The measured secondary prism sits on that curve at 230, 240 and
250 K.
It is faster at 220 K (119 against 101), at 260 K (63 against 52)
and at 265 K (50 against 37).
The quadratic has already turned down by 220 K and it falls faster
than these seeds on the warm side.
The text of the 2016 paper places the mW maximum around 40 K below
274.6 K, which is 235 K.
Shi, Fulford, Salvalaglio and Molteni describe that Espinosa
secondary-prism maximum as about 234.6 K.

Shi et al., Figure 3, is the basal face and the primary prism from
200 K to 270 K, ten replicas, with the maximum at 240 K on both
faces.
The markers read from that figure are unchanged: primary prism 98.3
\[85.2, 111.4\] at 240 K and 62.1 \[51.6, 72.7\] at 260 K, basal 88.1
\[76.4, 99.7\] and 39.5 \[27.2, 51.9\].
The primary-prism count slopes here, 104.7 \[93.3, 120.0\] and 57.7
\[52.3, 61.6\], overlap those bars.
The basal count slope at 260 K, 41.9 \[35.4, 46.8\], lies inside the
basal bar.
The basal count slope at 240 K, 65.8 \[57.6, 73.2\], lies below the
basal bar.
Their order parameter is the lq3 liquid count on a slab with a
quasi-liquid layer, and the earlier equation-2 speeds on this deck
were the ones that sat with the 240 K basal marker.
The maxima of the curves fit here are 229 K on the basal face and
225 K on the primary prism.
Neither interval reaches their stated 240 K maximum.
The count slopes at 240 K are still within a few angstroms per
nanosecond of the 230 K means on both faces.

Moore and Molinero, Nature 479, 506 (2011), do not tabulate a face
growth speed in Å/ns.
Espinosa et al. compare their brute-force crystallization times, for
about 4000 molecules and a frozen fraction 0.7, with the Avrami
estimate.
The minimum of those brute-force times is about ten nanoseconds.
The abstract places the mW minimum about 85 K below the melting
point, near 190 K, colder than every temperature run here.
At 220 K the one-front speeds are still at the top of the measured
curve, 119 Å/ns on the secondary prism, 101 on the primary prism and
58 on the basal face.
That is the growth factor inside the crystallization time, not the
crystallization time.

On one frame from the 240 K secondary prism, during the growth, the
pure-Python q6bar and the d-SEAMS q6bar counted the same molecules
above 0.30, 0.36, 0.40, 0.50 and 0.56.
The timing used eight frames from that secondary-prism trajectory,
spread through the run, repeated eight times.
The median and the interquartile range are over the eight repeats.
The per-frame time divides each repeat by eight.
At eight cores the Python baseline runs one process per frame.
d-SEAMS uses OpenMP with that many threads.

| tool | cores | per frame (ms) | IQR (ms) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| d-SEAMS CHILL+ | 1 | 7.92 | 0.12 |
| d-SEAMS q6bar | 1 | 4.99 | 0.08 |
| Python q6bar | 1 | 134.9 | 1.41 |
| d-SEAMS CHILL+ | 8 | 5.40 | 0.11 |
| d-SEAMS q6bar | 8 | 3.69 | 0.22 |
| Python q6bar | 8 | 32.9 | 2.57 |

On one core the Python q6bar takes 17 times the CHILL+ frame and 27
times the d-SEAMS q6bar frame.
Eight cores shorten the CHILL+ frame by a factor of 1.5 and the
d-SEAMS q6bar frame by a factor of 1.4.
The Python frame shortens by a factor of 4.1.

## On the shipped frames {#on-the-shipped-frames}

```bash
seams chill-plus input/traj/ice1h.lammpstrj --type 1 --rule chill+
seams chill-plus input/traj/ice1h.lammpstrj --type 1 --rule ovito-chill+
seams chill-plus input/traj/nucleation_f1.lammpstrj --type 1 --rule chill+
seams chill-plus input/traj/nucleation_f1.lammpstrj --type 1 --rule ovito-chill+
seams chill-plus input/traj/interface_f0.lammpstrj --type 1 --layers --axis 2
seams chill-plus input/traj/interface_f0.lammpstrj --type 1 --rule ovito-chill+
```

Ice Ih is hexagonal 128 under both rules.
The nucleation frame is the table in the nucleus section.
The interface slab is hexagonal 352, cubic 1, interfacial 49,
clathrate 3, interfacial clathrate 25, water 434 and stack
`HHHHHHHH....C.` under the published rule, and hexagonal 346, cubic 1,
interfacial 57, clathrate 3, interfacial clathrate 20 and water 437
under the OVITO rule.

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/linkcell-scaling.md -->

# Linkcell strong scaling {#linkcell-strong-scaling}

The linkcell manual is [linkcell.dseams.info](https://linkcell.dseams.info/).
This page is how d-SEAMS uses that library.

An orthorhombic frame is cut across ranks by linkcell’s weighted
recursive coordinate bisection of the periodic cell grid. d-SEAMS
passes that bisection. linkcell’s default method follows the bisection
with a Fiduccia-Mattheyses pass, and this cut does not request that
pass. A balance of zero selects `1 + parts * w_max / total`. `w_max`
is the heaviest cell weight and `total` is the sum of the cell
weights. That is the tightest bound a cell-aligned cut can promise.

Across those ranks, the first call weights each cell by how many
points it holds. A later call of CHILL+, of Steinhardt q6, or of the
primitive-ring census weights each cell by the work measured on the
first call. The cut is kept for a later call of that analysis with the
same atom count, box, halo, and rank count.

The halo is painted in the walk that visits the cells a rank owns. A
point in an owned cell stays owned. A point in a painted cell is a
ghost, and the rank that owns the cell owns the point.

A frame whose box is not three orthorhombic lengths keeps the slab,
pencil, or block cut. An orthorhombic frame whose mesh cannot be built
keeps that cut as well. A point inside the halo of the owned block is
a ghost.

## Inside one process {#inside-one-process}

One thread builds the cutoff list with linkcell’s fused kernel. From
outside a running team, two or more threads build an orthorhombic list
on one shared cell grid. Each thread takes a contiguous run of
columns, and the runs split the atoms evenly. A pair whose columns
both lie in one run is tested once and written into both rows. A pair
that crosses a run is tested from each side, and each side writes its
own row. The cell counts and the row storage stay allocated and are
rewritten on the next call. Below 2048 atoms in the list, this builder
runs on one thread.

With two or more threads, a restricted triclinic box uses the tilted
cell list. CHILL+, Steinhardt q6, and the primitive-ring census read
these rows. The pair set does not depend on the thread count.


---

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/ovito-findrings.md -->

# Primitive rings and OVITO FindRings {#primitive-rings-and-ovito-findrings}

A ring is primitive when every pair of its vertices is as close along
the ring as it is through the rest of the graph. That is Franzblau’s
shortest-path test (Phys. Rev. B 44, 4925, 1991). OVITO’s
`FindRingsModifier` is a shortest-path census of the same kind of
ring. On the frames where both searches stop at six-membered rings
the two counts agree. `FindRings` can also drop a chordless ring that
the Franzblau test keeps.

## The same bond graph {#the-same-bond-graph}

Both searches on this page use one cutoff, 3.5 Å, and the minimum
image of the periodic cell. A pair is a bond when its squared
distance is strictly below the squared cutoff. Compare the bond lists
first. The ring counts are a comparison of the ring definitions when
the two bond lists are the same.

## K2,3 {#k2-3}

Five vertices and six edges. Label the two parts $\{0,3\}$ and
$\{1,2,4\}$, and join every vertex of the first part to every
vertex of the second. There is no edge inside either part, so none
of the three 4-cycles has a chord:

- $0-1-3-2$
- $0-1-3-4$
- $0-2-3-4$

Each pair of opposite vertices on those cycles is at distance 2 in
the graph, which is the ring distance. All three cycles are
primitive. `ringNetwork` with maximum size 4 returns the three.
`FindRings` with the same six bonds and maximum size 4 returns two.
The missing cycle is primitive. The smaller count is a ring the
search did not emit.

## The interface frame {#the-interface-frame}

`input/traj/interface_f0.lammpstrj` is orthorhombic, 864 atoms, all
of type 1. At 3.5 Å the cutoff graph has 1929 bonds.
`ringNetwork` with maximum size 10 returns 2662 rings. Every one of
them passes the Franzblau test: for every pair, the shorter arc is a
breadth-first distance in that 1929-bond graph.

| size | rings |
| --- | --- |
| 3 | 142 |
| 4 | 188 |
| 5 | 377 |
| 6 | 1143 |
| 7 | 257 |
| 8 | 54 |
| 9 | 52 |
| 10 | 449 |

The depth-6 bins are 188, 377 and 1143, and `FindRings` on this frame
at maximum size 6 reports those three counts. Across sizes 4 through 10,
the bond counts match, every d-SEAMS ring is primitive, and each OVITO
bin is at most the primitive bin. K2,3 is the strict
subset: 3 primitive 4-rings, and `FindRings` reports 2. Agreement at
size 6 on this frame leaves the larger bins to that inequality.

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/performance.md -->

# Release-candidate sitting {#release-candidate-sitting}

The tables are the release-candidate sitting of d-SEAMS 2.14.0.
Ideal ice Ic supplies the neighbour list, $q_4$, $q_6$, CHILL+,
the ring search, and the row stored as PTM, at 110592 and 884736
molecules. Cages are GenIce sI (46 molecules), sII (136), and the
sI 2x2x2 cell (368). King’s shortest-path count is the fastatomstruct
table.

One warm-up is discarded. `n` is 6 on every row. The median of an even
count is the mean of the two central samples. The interquartile range
is the type-7 gap: the linear quantile at 0.75 minus the linear
quantile at 0.25.

`threads` is the width of that row. The worker starts with
`OMP_NUM_THREADS` set to that width and `OMP_DYNAMIC=FALSE`. One
thread is pinned with `taskset -c 0`. Eight threads are pinned with
`taskset -c 0-7`. `cores` is the affinity list recorded for the timed
process. freud, mdapy, vesin, OVITO, and rings-statistics-matter then
receive that width through their own setters. The PLUMED worker sets
`OMP_NUM_THREADS` and does not set `PLUMED_NUM_THREADS`. Its observable
is $Q_l$ with a rational switch, `R_0` 0.35, `D_MAX` 0.35, `NN` 100
and `MM` 200, multiplied by the square root of $4\pi/(2l+1)$.

The d-SEAMS rings call is `seams_frame_rings` on the cutoff graph, depth
6, so the neighbour list and the search are one timed call. The rows at
1000, 4096, 10648, 21952, 32768 and 64000 molecules are the reference
stored beside King’s count. A King size is stored only when the call
returns inside 600 seconds. At 110592 molecules the rings block stores
two d-SEAMS rows, both with `n` of 6. The table does not mark which of
those two is the head-to-head call and which is the King reference.
The 884736-molecule rings row is the head-to-head call.

The d-SEAMS row stored as PTM is `seams_frame_symmetry` with shell RMSD
0.12. The OVITO row stored as PTM is `PolyhedralTemplateMatchingModifier`
with structure ids 6 and 7 enabled.

Ice and a TIP4P/ice liquid at 884736 molecules, with widths 1, 2, 4
and 8, are [the head-to-head](performance-h2h.md).
Neighbour and ring rows from the other records are
[the size range](performance-range.md).
What each sitting measures is
[the overview](performance-overview.md).

The algorithm pages are
[primitive rings](primitive-rings.md),
[TRACE and signature cages](trace-assembly.md),
[the symmetry classifier](symmetry.md), and
[carried rings](hop-ball.md).
The signature-search widths are
[thread controls](trace-threads.md).

| Medians and interquartile ranges from six timed calls after one warm-up. |
| --- |

# Performance {#performance}

Head-to-head times for ice Ic and a TIP4P/ice liquid at 884736
molecules. The widths are 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads. `n` is the sample
count on the row. Liquid rings-statistics-matter at one thread has
`n` of 6. Every other row of this sitting has `n` of 8. The median
and the interquartile range are recomputed from the samples.

The figure is median time against thread count, ice and liquid side
by side. The vertical axis is logarithmic. It draws neighbours, rings,
$q_6$ and CHILL+.

The rings rows are `seams_frame_rings` on the cutoff graph, depth 6:
the neighbour list and the search are one timed call. The last table
is a separate comparison of that full call, linkcell against the cell
list. `n` is 8 on each of those rows. The link, convert and search
stages of the same comparison are on
[the thread controls](trace-threads.md).

The release-candidate comparison, including cages and King’s count, is
[the sitting page](performance.md).
Neighbour and ring rows for 4096 to 110592
molecules are on [the size range](performance-range.md).
How the comparisons differ is on
[the overview](performance-overview.md).

![Median time against thread count for 884736 molecules](../_images/sitting-large-threads.svg)

*Ice and the TIP4P/ice liquid. Each line is one code. The vertical axis is logarithmic.*

| Ice Ic and the TIP4P/ice liquid, 884736 molecules, at 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads. median_ms and iqr_ms are recomputed from samples_ms. |
| --- |

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/performance-overview.md -->

# Performance overview {#performance-overview}

Each median is printed on one page.

| page | comparison |
| --- | --- |
| Release-candidate sitting | Ideal ice Ic at 110592 and 884736 molecules, one thread and eight. n is 6. Median and type-7 interquartile range for neighbours, q_4, q_6, CHILL+, rings, cages, the row stored as PTM, and King’s count. |
| Head-to-head | Ice Ic and a TIP4P/ice liquid at 884736 molecules, at 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads. n is 6 or 8. Median and interquartile range recomputed from the samples. |
| 4096 to 110592 | Neighbour and ring rows for 4096 to 110592 molecules, kept when n is at least 6, with the recorded interval. |
| Signature thread controls | The hydrate signature search, the eight kernels, and the cutoff ring call split into link, convert and search. |

The operation string is the string the table stored. It is a different call on different pages.

On the release-candidate comparison, $q_4$ and $q_6$ are one Steinhardt call, and the rings row is `seams_frame_rings` on the cutoff graph: the neighbour list and the search together. The 884736-molecule rings row is that same call in the other comparison. The rings kernel on the thread-controls page is `ringNetwork` after the neighbour graph already exists. Those ring times are separate measurements.

The release-candidate PLUMED worker sets `OMP_NUM_THREADS` and does not set `PLUMED_NUM_THREADS`. The head-to-head page holds the other PLUMED $q_6$ rows.


---

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/performance-range.md -->

# Performance, 4096 to 110592 {#performance-4096-to-110592}

Neighbour lists and primitive rings from the comparisons other
than the release-candidate sitting and the 884736-molecule head-to-head.
A row is listed when its stored `n` is at least 6. The interval is
`q1 ms` and `q3 ms` when recorded, `iqr ms` when that is
the recorded interval, and `min ms` when that is the second time
recorded. The version column is the version the row recorded. Two of the tables store a variant
column, `rings` or `bonds_and_rings`.

One cycless comparison also stores a 1000-molecule row. It is listed with
that table. Rows whose stored `n` is below 6 are omitted.

The release-candidate medians are on
[the sitting page](performance.md).
The 884736-molecule ice and liquid medians are on
[the head-to-head](performance-h2h.md).
What each comparison measures is on
[the overview](performance-overview.md).

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/primitive-rings.md -->

# Primitive rings and the full graph {#primitive-rings-and-the-full-graph}

A ring is primitive when the graph distance between every pair of its
vertices equals the shorter distance along the ring. That is Franzblau’s
shortest-path test. A chordless ring can fail it: the missing shortcut
need not be an edge of the ring.

## Distances, then the source {#distances-then-the-source}

The search builds a ring from one source, the lowest-indexed member of
that ring. Two facts have to hold at once.

Distances are taken on the whole graph. A shortcut may pass through a
vertex whose index is below the source. Hiding that vertex makes the
opposite vertex look farther away than it is, and a ring that is not
primitive is kept.

After those distances are known, every vertex below the source loses
its level. No path is extended through that vertex, so it is not
written onto a ring this source emits. The ring is still reported once,
from its lowest member.

## Worked example {#worked-example}

Number the vertices of a hexagon `1-2-3-4-5-6`, and join a new vertex
`0` to the opposite vertices `1` and `4`.

A walk that refuses to enter vertex `0` reports distance 3 between 1
and 4. The hexagon then looks primitive, because each pair appears to
sit at its ring distance.

The full graph has the path `1-0-4`, so the distance is 2. The ring
distance is 3, and the hexagon is not primitive. The two pentagons
`0-1-2-3-4` and `0-1-6-5-4` are primitive. A chordless search keeps the
hexagon as well, because no edge joins two non-consecutive vertices of
the hexagon. The primitive search rejects the hexagon and keeps the
pentagons.

The same search matches an
independent enumeration of the primitive cycles. Where
`FindRings` drops a primitive ring, the K2,3 counterexample is on
[Primitive rings and OVITO FindRings](ovito-findrings.md).

## The shortest-path statement {#the-shortest-path-statement}

Yuan and Cormack (Comput. Mater. Sci. 24, 343, 2002) build each ring
from shortest paths. A ring of even size $2L$ is a source plus two
vertex-disjoint shortest paths to one vertex at level $L$. A ring of
odd size $2L+1$ closes on an edge that joins two vertices both at
level $L$. The search builds those candidates only up to the largest
size requested. In the code that limit is `maxDepth`, and the breadth-first
walk stops at level `maxDepth / 2`.

Franzblau’s filter then drops a candidate when any pair of its members
is closer through the graph than along the ring. For a cycle
$(v_0,\ldots,v_{n-1})$,

$$
d_G(v_i, v_j) = \min_{k \in \mathbb{Z}} |i - j + kn|
$$

must hold for every pair, with $d_G$ the breadth-first distance on
the whole neighbour graph. The search reports each ring once, from its
lowest index, and sorts the list lexicographically. The output depends
on the graph, not on the order of the rows.

The installed call is `seams_rings_find` in `seams.h`. The language
ABI is `seams_frame_rings`. The CLI is `seams rings`.

The signatures are on [C](../stable/c.md) and [C++](../stable/cpp.md).


---

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/ring-completion.md -->

# Ring-adjacent completion {#ring-adjacent-completion}

`ring::ringAdjacentCompletion` fills a single vacancy on a labeled
six-ring. `ring::seededCageAffiliation` has two overloads. The one
that computes the affiliation takes the completion flag as its fifth
argument, a `bool` named `ringAdjacentCompletion`, default `false`.
The overload that receives a precomputed affiliation puts the same
flag last. Cage flags are hexagonal cage (HC) and double-diamond cage
(DDC).

## The all-but-one rule {#the-all-but-one-rule}

Take the per-atom HC or DDC flags from a seeded pass and the
six-membered rings of the permissive graph. A ring whose vertices all
carry that cage label but one is a cage ring with a vacancy. The last
vertex takes the label. The walk repeats until a fixed point. The HC
flags and the DDC flags run as two walks.

A liquid six-ring that touches a nucleus has at most a few labeled
vertices. Five labeled vertices are required, so the walk cannot
enter the liquid. An empty seed stays empty.

## The flag on `seededCageAffiliation` {#the-flag-on-seededcageaffiliation}

```c++
ring::SeededAtomLabels seededCageAffiliation(
    const std::vector<std::vector<int>> &strictRings,
    const std::vector<std::vector<int>> &strictNList,
    const std::vector<std::vector<int>> &permissiveRings,
    const std::vector<std::vector<int>> &permissiveNList,
    bool ringAdjacentCompletion = false);
```

When the flag is `false` (the default), the function returns the
seeded labels. When the flag is `true`, those labels pass through
`ring::ringAdjacentCompletion` on `permissiveRings`.

`seams cages --complete` sets the flag.

On cubic ice the walk leaves both flag vectors unchanged. Clearing
one atom’s label on that crystal fills it again. An empty seed stays
empty.

## Least fixed point {#least-fixed-point}

The labeled set is the least fixed point of the all-but-one rule
above the seed. Visiting order does not change that set.

Edge-sharing is a different rule. It labels every vertex of a ring
that shares two vertices with a fully labeled ring, so two shared
vertices label the rest of that ring. Those vertices stay unlabeled
under the all-but-one closure.


---

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/rings-one-thread.md -->

# Rings on one thread {#rings-on-one-thread}

`primitive::ringNetwork` against OVITO 3.17.2 `FindRingsModifier`.
The cutoff graph is built before the timer on both sides.
The cutoff is 3.5 Å and the largest ring has 6 members.
Eight timed calls follow two warmups. The median of those eight
is the mean of the two central samples.
The table rounds each median to 0.001 ms.

## Frames {#frames}

| name | molecules | frame |
| --- | --- | --- |
| tri-136 | 136 | input/traj/genice_sH.lammpstrj, guest-free structure H |
| orth-4k | 4096 | input/traj/mW_cubic.lammpstrj, cubic ice |
| orth-1e5 | 110592 | that cubic cell, replicated 3 by 3 by 3 |

The per-size census is the same in both codes.

| molecules | 4 | 5 | 6 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 136 | 12 | 120 | 68 |
| 4096 | 0 | 0 | 8192 |
| 110592 | 0 | 0 | 221184 |

## Measured times {#measured-times}

The build is a release build with OpenMP on 8 cores. OVITO is 3.17.2.

| molecules | threads | d-SEAMS (ms) | OVITO (ms) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 136 | 1 | 0.183 | 0.534 |
| 4096 | 1 | 2.363 | 13.354 |
| 110592 | 1 | 68.773 | 415.508 |
| 136 | 8 | 0.187 | 0.541 |
| 4096 | 8 | 3.601 | 13.230 |
| 110592 | 8 | 19.874 | 358.581 |

The one-thread medians are lower for d-SEAMS at each of the three
sizes, and so are the eight-thread medians.

## Search {#search}

The timed call asks for rings of at most 6 members. A strict shortcut
on a ring of at most 7 members is a walk of one or two edges, read
from the neighbour rows, so this search never builds a distance ball.
The rings are the Franzblau set.


---

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/sqq.md -->

# SQQ {#sqq}

SQQ 0.5.8 counts shortest-path chordless rings of size 4, 5 and 6.
d-SEAMS 2.14.0 counts primitive rings, and that census includes
3-rings, which SQQ does not search. On a crystal the two censuses
are the same list. On a disordered hydrogen-bond network they are
not, and an ice label that reads those rings moves with them.

The ice comparison has three readings. The merged label puts
published CHILL+, which does not search rings, next to SQQ’s ice
stage on chordless 6-rings. The primitive reading applies that same
SQQ ice rule to the d-SEAMS primitive 6-rings. The chordless reading
applies it to the d-SEAMS chordless 6-rings. The chordless reading
is the like-for-like label. The merged reading is the whole-tool
label.

## The 4096-molecule TIP4P/2005 frame {#the-4096-molecule-tip4p-2005-frame}

The oxygen-oxygen edges and the rings match.

| quantity | d-SEAMS | SQQ | agreement |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| O-O edges | 10495 | 10495 | 1 |
| 4-rings | 1758 | 1758 | 1 |
| 5-rings | 2763 | 2763 | 1 |
| 6-rings | 2485 | 2485 | 1 |
| chordless 6-rings | 4045 | 4045 | 1 |

The merged ice label does not. Published CHILL+ names 4 molecules
ice and SQQ names 1129. The agreement is 0.724854. The SQQ rule on
the primitive 6-rings names 1075, agreement 0.986816 against SQQ’s

1. The same rule on the chordless 6-rings names 1129 on both

sides, agreement 1, all 4096 molecules.

The ring lists already match, so the merged gap is the choice of
ice rule. CHILL+ reads four bond correlations. SQQ reads the
chordless 6-rings. Once both sides use the chordless rings, the
labels agree.

Eight repeats, mean milliseconds. The ratio is SQQ divided by d-SEAMS.

| operation | threads | d-SEAMS | SQQ | ratio |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| rings | 1 | 22.6026 | 1054.3846 | 46.649 |
| rings | 8 | 8.2165 | 1056.0863 | 128.532 |
| ice, CHILL+ against SQQ | 1 | 1.7860 | 914.2565 | 511.905 |
| ice, CHILL+ against SQQ | 8 | 1.5802 | 916.2551 | 579.849 |
| ice, chordless rings | 1 | 28.5570 | 914.2565 | 32.015 |
| ice, chordless rings | 8 | 7.9694 | 916.2551 | 114.971 |

SQQ is one Python process. Extra threads do not shorten it. The
d-SEAMS ring search does shorten, so the ratio rises from one
thread to eight.

## Where else the lists agree {#where-else-the-lists-agree}

Ideal ice Ic and ice Ih, at 4096 and at 110592 molecules, match on
the edges, the 4-rings, the 5-rings, the 6-rings, the chordless
6-rings and every ice reading. Each crystal has two 6-rings per
molecule and no 4-ring or 5-ring.

The 4096-molecule mW liquid matches on the edges and the rings.
Its merged ice agreement is 0.561768 (81 against 1851). The
chordless reading matches, 1851 on both sides.

The 250-molecule TIP4P oxygen frame matches on the edges and the
rings. Its merged ice agreement is 0.176000 (0 against 206). The
chordless reading matches, 206 on both sides.

The 110592-molecule mW liquid is the frame that misses. The
oxygen-oxygen edges are 259187 and 259186. The 4-rings are 34097
and 34098, the 5-rings 86218 and 86217, the 6-rings 85092 and
85094, and the chordless 6-rings 123915 and 123917. The chordless
ice reading is 50120 against 50121, agreement 0.999991. The merged
ice agreement is 0.561957.

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/stacking-disorder.md -->

# Stacking disorder {#stacking-disorder}

Cubic ice and hexagonal ice are the same puckered hexagons stacked in
two orders. Hexagonal ice repeats every two layers. Cubic ice repeats
every three, and the next layer sits over the hole of the one before.
A stacking fault is one layer in the other order. Both crystals, and
the fault between them, have a high local $q_6$. A cutoff on $q_6$
therefore reports ice and stops.

Two counts in this tree keep the polytypes apart.

The cage census names the cages. A hexagonal layer is a six-ring that
is the base of a hexagonal cage: two basal faces and three prismatic
faces. A cubic layer is a six-ring that closes a double-diamond cage.
A molecule that belongs to both cages is `both`. The rest of each cage
is `hexagonal` or `cubic`. None of those names is a threshold on
$q_6$. `seams cages` prints the four counts.

```bash
seams cages input/traj/interface_f0.lammpstrj --type 1
```

On that 864-molecule slab the seeded graph and the cutoff graph both
print hexagonal 444, cubic 0, `both` 0 and water 420. The mutual graph
prints hexagonal 442, cubic 0, `both` 0 and water 422. The one cubic molecule in the slab is not a
double-diamond cage, and no molecule sits in both cages.

CHILL+ names hexagonal and cubic from the bond correlations, and
`--layers` writes the stack along the long edge. The published rule is
the 2015 table. The account of that rule is
[CHILL+: the published rule and the OVITO rule](chill-plus-rules.md).

```bash
seams chill-plus input/traj/interface_f0.lammpstrj --type 1 --layers --axis 2
```

The frame is the one in
[the interface tutorial](../user/tutorials/interface.md).
The command prints hexagonal 352, cubic 1 and water 434, and the stack
`HHHHHHHH....C.`: eight hexagonal slabs, a gap, and one cubic layer.
A $q_6$ cutoff would add the 352 and the 1. The stack string keeps
them apart, which is what a growth rate on the basal face needs. The
front advances by a layer of one polytype. The fault is that layer.

The same split is why a nucleation frame reports cubic and hexagonal
counts separately. On `input/traj/nucleation_f1.lammpstrj` the published
rule prints hexagonal 62 and cubic 47. The largest crystal cluster can
contain both, and the fraction of each says which polytype the nucleus
is growing. $q_6$ on that cluster is one number.


---

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/symmetry.md -->

# Local symmetry {#local-symmetry}

The classifier names each oxygen as ice Ih, ice Ic, stacking-disordered
ice, or unmatched, and it can name a hydrate cage or a five- or six-ring
when one cluster is passed in. The per-atom ice label is the production
path. The command and the per-atom call are on
[the symmetry classifier](../user/howto/symmetry-classifier.md).

A crystal oxygen is ice Ih (0), ice Ic (1), or stacking-disordered ice
(2). Anything else is -1. The seventeen-atom shell is the central
oxygen, its four nearest neighbours, and the twelve neighbours of those
four. That is the shell polyhedral template matching uses for diamond
(Larsen, Schmidt and Schiøtz, *Modelling and Simulation in Materials Science and Engineering* 24, 055007, 2016,
DOI 10.1088/0965-0393/24/5/055007,
[arXiv:1603.05143](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.05143)).

## Neighbours {#neighbours}

The bond cutoff is 3.5 Å. A neighbour closer than 2.15 Å is dropped.
The four nearest bonds are kept. One thread walks each pair once, using
half of the 27-cell stencil, and writes both ends of the bond. Several
threads scan the full stencil and write one end. When the cell is
orthorhombic and every edge is at least three bond lengths, the atoms
are wrapped into the box and histogrammed into cells of that cutoff.
A skewed cell uses a wider stencil. The coordinate columns are reused
on the next frame of the same size.

A center whose four bonds do not all lie between 2.30 Å and 3.35 Å is
left unmatched, and the second shell is not read.

## Tetrahedral order {#tetrahedral-order}

The tetrahedral order parameter $q$ is the Chau–Hardwick /
Errington–Debenedetti invariant of the four bonds (Errington and
Debenedetti, *Nature* 409, 318, 2001,
[10.1038/35053024](https://doi.org/10.1038/35053024)). With
$\theta_{jk}$ the angle at the center between neighbours $j$ and
$k$,

$$
q = 1 - \frac{3}{8}
\sum_{j=1}^{3} \sum_{k=j+1}^{4}
\left(\cos\theta_{jk} + \frac{1}{3}\right)^{2}.
$$

Equal bonds skip this test. An ideal crystal has equal bonds, and the
staggered test below names it. Otherwise a center with $q < 0.85$ is
left unmatched and the second shell is not read. The library constant
is `kThermalQ`.

## Common-neighbour fingerprint {#common-neighbour-fingerprint}

The second shell is the adaptive-cutoff common-neighbour signature of
Maras, Trushin, Stukowski, Albe and Nordlund, *Computer Physics Communications* 205, 13 (2016), Appendix A
([10.1016/j.cpc.2016.04.001](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cpc.2016.04.001)).
The cutoff for a bond of length $r$ is $r(1+\sqrt{2})/2$.

Twelve $(4,2,1)$ patterns are ice Ic. Six $(4,2,1)$ and six
$(4,2,2)$ are ice Ih. A partial cubic signature needs at least eight
good patterns, at least as many $(4,2,1)$ as $(4,2,2)$, at least
eight $(4,2,1)$, and $q \ge 0.97$. Six or seven $(4,2,1)$
patterns are not labeled cubic. With $q \ge 0.97$ they are passed
to the fit. Below that, the fit runs only when the conditions in the
next section hold. A partial
hexagonal signature needs at least eight good patterns, more
$(4,2,2)$ than $(4,2,1)$, at least four $(4,2,2)$, and the same
$q \ge 0.97$.

A second shell whose radii differ by more than a factor 1.45 does not
receive this signature. It can still be fitted when $q \ge 0.85$, the
longest of the four bonds is at most 1.20 times the shortest, and the
second-shell radii differ by at most a factor 1.6.

An ideal shell, equal bonds and one second-shell radius, is named from
the raw cosine of each second-shell bond with another first-shell bond
and does not build this signature. The bond vectors are not projected.
On the ideal cell that cosine is $1/3$ for a staggered arm and $7/9$
for an eclipsed arm. The fast path compares the squares, $1/9$ and
$49/81$. An arm is eclipsed when the best square is at least 0.36,
and staggered when that square is at most 0.25. Four staggered arms are
ice Ic. One eclipsed arm and three staggered arms are ice Ih.

## The fit {#the-fit}

A shell is fitted when the fingerprint did not name it, it already has
one crystal neighbour, $q \ge 0.85$, the longest bond is at most 1.20
times the shortest, and the second-shell radius varies by at most a
factor 1.6. Both clouds are centered. The optimal rotation is a
quaternion (Horn, *Journal of the Optical Society of America A* 4, 629,
1987, [10.1364/JOSAA.4.000629](https://doi.org/10.1364/JOSAA.4.000629);
Coutsias, Seok and Dill, *Journal of Computational Chemistry* 25, 1849,
2004, [10.1002/jcc.20110](https://doi.org/10.1002/jcc.20110)). The
residual is the root-mean-square distance after that rotation, divided
by the template radius, the normalization Larsen, Schmidt and Schiøtz
use. Zero is a perfect shape. The ceiling is `kShellRmsd`, 0.15:

$$
\frac{\mathrm{RMSD}}{R_{\mathrm{template}}} \le 0.15.
$$

`seams symmetry` uses that ceiling. A positive `shell_rmsd` on
`seams_system_symmetry` or `seams_symmetry_classify_tol` replaces it.
A non-positive value selects 0.15 again.

The bond-angle fingerprint names the one template the fit tries. This
cosine is the azimuthal one: both bonds are projected onto the plane
perpendicular to the central bond. Ideal staggered ice lies at 60
degrees, cosine $1/2$, and ideal eclipsed ice lies at 0 degrees,
cosine 1. An arm above 0.90 is eclipsed. Four eclipsed arms are left
unmatched, except on the recovery pass, where that pattern is
hexagonal. The eclipsed arm is anchored to the eclipsed arm of the
template. The four-point orientation uses one Jacobi sweep and the
seventeen-atom residual uses two. A shell that is still far after a few
correspondences is left unmatched, and a shell with only one crystal
neighbour is abandoned sooner than a shell with two.

After the labels are written, a crystal atom that has no crystal
neighbour among its four bonds is returned to unmatched. Hexagonal
recovery is one pass over the atoms left unmatched. It tries an atom
that already has three crystal neighbours, and on that pass four
eclipsed arms can be ice Ih.

## Cages, rings, and the other codes {#cages-rings-and-the-other-codes}

The same in-tree matcher names a cage or a ring. It is a 3×3 SVD with
the permutation fixed by the bond graph. The continuous shape measure
of that overlay is the scaled residual of Pinsky and Avnir (*Inorganic Chemistry* 37, 5575, 1998,
[10.1021/ic9804925](https://doi.org/10.1021/ic9804925)) and of the
Alvarez shape measure (*Coordination Chemistry Reviews* 249, 1693,
2005, [10.1016/j.ccr.2005.03.031](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ccr.2005.03.031)).

IRA (Gunde, Salles, Hémeryck and Martin-Samos, *Journal of Chemical Information and Modeling* 61, 5446, 2021,
[10.1021/acs.jcim.1c00567](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jcim.1c00567))
is an optional second matcher for the same templates. SOFI, from the
same group (*Journal of Chemical Physics* 161, 062503, 2024,
[10.1063/5.0215689](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0215689)), names the
point group. spglib (Togo, Shinohara and Tanaka, *Science and Technology of Advanced Materials: Methods* 4, 2384822, 2024,
[10.1080/27660400.2024.2384822](https://doi.org/10.1080/27660400.2024.2384822))
names the space group. CHILL+ (Nguyen and Molinero, *Journal of Physical Chemistry B* 119, 9369, 2015,
[10.1021/jp510289t](https://doi.org/10.1021/jp510289t)) is a different
label. The two CHILL+ rules are on
[CHILL+: the published rule and the OVITO rule](chill-plus-rules.md).

A build uses IRA and SOFI when libira is linked, and spglib when
libsymspg is linked. Without libira the matcher is the in-tree Kabsch
search. `pointGroup` returns status 2 when SOFI is absent.
`spaceGroup` returns status 2 when spglib is absent, and
`seams symmetry` then prints `space-group off`.

## What the command prints {#what-the-command-prints}

`seams symmetry` prints the matcher, a space-group line, one shell
overlay when a crystal shell exists, and the tally. The names are
`ice-Ih`, `ice-Ic`, `ice-Isd`, and `unmatched`.

```bash
seams symmetry input/traj/ice1h.lammpstrj --type 1
seams symmetry input/traj/mW_cubic.lammpstrj --type 1
```

On the 128-molecule ice Ih cell the tally is `shells ice-Ih 128 unmatched 0`. On the 4096-molecule mW cubic cell it is `shells ice-Ic 4096 unmatched 0`. A build without libira reports `symmetry backend kabsch`.

The same call on the shipped frames, with this ceiling:

| frame | molecules | ice Ih | ice Ic | stacking-disordered | unmatched |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| interface_f0.lammpstrj | 864 | 245 | 0 | 0 | 619 |
| nucleation_f1.lammpstrj | 4096 | 8 | 12 | 1 | 4075 |

Published CHILL+ on those frames is a wider crystal. The interface slab
is hexagonal 352, cubic 1, interfacial 49, clathrate 3, interfacial
clathrate 25 and water 434. The nucleation frame is hexagonal 62, cubic
47, interfacial 240, clathrate 20, interfacial clathrate 138 and water

1. CHILL+ cubic and hexagonal need four bond correlations in the

staggered or eclipsed windows. The shell also asks for the
common-neighbour signature or a residual at most 0.15, and for a
crystal neighbour. CHILL+ has an interfacial label. The shell does not,
so two or three staggered bonds stay unmatched.

C++, in `symm`, `classifyIce` writes one label per row. The default
ceiling is `kShellRmsd` (0.15), the tetrahedral cutoff is `kThermalQ`
(0.85), and the bond-length ratio is `kThermalBondRatio` (1.20).
`classifyIceArrays` is the same call on three coordinate columns.
`best`, `matchKernel` and `matchAll` name one environment. The template
names are `ice-Ih`, `ice-Ic`, `ice-Isd`, `5^12`, `5^12 6^2`,
`5^12 6^4`, `ring-5` and `ring-6`.

C, in `seams_c_api.h`, `seams_symmetry_classify` writes the same labels
at the library ceiling. `seams_symmetry_classify_tol` takes an explicit
ceiling. `seams_symmetry_classify_gates` also takes the tetrahedral
cutoff and the bond-length ratio.

Python is `dseams.symmetry` in
[PydSEAMSlib](https://github.com/d-SEAMS/PydSEAMSlib).
The per-atom integers are the ones above.


---

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/topological-network.md -->

# Topological network criteria {#topological-network-criteria}

These are the criteria the classifiers use.
Worked counts are in the
[rings](../user/tutorials/rings.md),
[bulk ice](../user/tutorials/bulk-ice.md),
[order parameter](../user/tutorials/order-parameters.md) and
[confined water](../user/tutorials/confined-water.md) tutorials.
The two CHILL+ rules are compared on
[CHILL+: the published rule and the OVITO rule](chill-plus-rules.md).

## Bond correlation {#bond-correlation}

CHILL and CHILL+ look at $l = 3$.
With $N_b(i)$ neighbours,

$$
q_{3m}(i) = \frac{1}{N_b(i)} \sum_{j \in N(i)} Y_{3m}(\hat r_{ij})
$$

$$
c_{ij} = \mathrm{Re}
\frac{\sum_m q_{3m}(i)\, q_{3m}(j)^{*}}
{\sqrt{\sum_m |q_{3m}(i)|^2 \sum_m |q_{3m}(j)|^2}}
$$

A bond is staggered when $c_{ij} \le -0.8$.
The eclipsed window is the part that differs:

| rule | eclipsed | staggered | neighbours |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| CHILL | -0.2 \le c_{ij} \le -0.05 | c_{ij} \le -0.8 | 4 |
| CHILL+ | -0.35 \le c_{ij} \le 0.25 | c_{ij} \le -0.8 | 4 |

The code stores those edges as `chill::chillRule` `(-0.8, -0.2, -0.05, 4)` and `chill::chillPlusRule` `(-0.8, -0.35, 0.25, 4)`.
For those two rules the boundaries are inclusive.
`ovito-chill+` uses the CHILL+ numbers with open edges:
$c_{ij} < -0.8$ is staggered, and the eclipsed window is open at both ends.

The four-bond star is the phase.
Both published rules read the four nearest neighbours.
CHILL labels from that star even when a fifth oxygen lies inside the cutoff.
CHILL+ first requires the cutoff shell itself to hold exactly four neighbours, so that fifth oxygen is water.
The average in Nguyen and Molinero, equation 1 (J. Phys. Chem. B 2015, 119, 9369), is still over the four nearest,

$$
q_{lm}(i) = \frac{1}{4} \sum_{j=1}^{4} Y_{lm}(\hat r_{ij}).
$$

With four bonds the phases are:

| phase | eclipsed | staggered | further test |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| cubic | 0 | 4 |  |
| hexagonal | 1 | 3 |  |
| interfacial |  | 2 | a neighbour has more than two staggered bonds |
| interfacial | 0 | 3 | CHILL: a neighbour has exactly two staggered bonds. CHILL+: a neighbour has more than one |
| clathrate | 4 | 0 | CHILL+ only |
| interfacial clathrate | 3 |  | CHILL+ only |
| water |  |  | every remaining atom |

CHILL has no clathrate row.
An atom whose recorded bond count is not 4 is water under both rules.
`bop.hpp` lists the same phase names, and `chill::isInterfacial` is the neighbour test in the two interfacial rows.

`ovito-chill+` (`--rule ovito-chill+`, or the `ovito-chill+` command) is the OVITO 3.17.2 Chill+ modifier.
A crystal row still requires exactly four neighbours inside the cutoff.
$q_3$ is averaged over every neighbour in that shell, the edges are the open cuts above, and the interfacial rows do not consult a neighbour.
Two staggered bonds, or three staggered bonds and no eclipsed bond, are interfacial.

## Primitive rings {#primitive-rings}

A cycle is primitive, in the Franzblau sense, when for every pair of its vertices a shortest path in the bond graph lies along the cycle.
`primitive::ringNetwork` returns the primitive cycles whose size is at most `max_depth`.
The bond graph is an argument.
Mutual k-nearest, the union of those nominations, and a distance cutoff are three different graphs.
Quote the graph with the census.

## Cages {#cages}

A hexagonal cage is two basal six-rings and three prismatic six-rings.
A double-diamond cage is one equatorial six-ring and six peripheral rings.
`ring::cageAffiliation` evaluates those conditions for every six-ring.
`findHC` and `findDDC` claim rings as they accept them, so which rings they test depends on visiting order.
The affiliation predicates evaluate every six-ring.

The seeded variant takes a strict graph for the seeds and a permissive graph for the completions.
An atom on the permissive graph is kept only when its component contains a seed.
`--complete` then fills a six-ring that is missing one labeled vertex.
That walk is the least fixed point of the all-but-one rule, on
[Ring-adjacent completion](ring-completion.md).

## Confined ice {#confined-ice}

A prism block is two rings of the same size.
`ring::basalPrismConditions` is the strict test, and a pair that passes is perfect.
With shape matching on, a pair that fails that test is imperfect when `ring::relaxedPrismConditions` finds at least one bond between the rings and the shape match succeeds.
`ring::findPrisms` returns the rings that are blocks and the perfect and imperfect counts.

A monolayer analysis keeps primitive rings of each size and writes the coverage of the sheet.
The in-plane $g(r)$ normalises the pair histogram by the slab factor

$$
f(r) = 1 - \frac{r}{2h} \quad (r \le h), \qquad f(r) = \frac{h}{2r} \quad (r > h)
$$

where $h$ is the confined height.
That is `rdf2::normalizeRDF`.

## Order parameters {#order-parameters}

$$
q_l(i) = \sqrt{\frac{4\pi}{2l+1} \sum_{m=-l}^{l} |q_{lm}(i)|^2}
$$

$\bar q_l(i)$ replaces $q_{lm}(i)$ with the average of $q_{lm}$ over $i$ and its neighbours before the same sum.
That is the Lechner-Dellago form.
The implementation is `chill::steinhardtQl`.
It computes degrees 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12.
Other degrees return zeros.


---

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/trace-assembly.md -->

# TRACE and signature cages {#trace-and-signature-cages}

TRACE (Hsu and Lin, J. Chem. Theory Comput. 2025,
[10.1021/acs.jctc.5c01459](https://doi.org/10.1021/acs.jctc.5c01459))
finds hydrate cages on a hydrogen-bond graph. d-SEAMS answers the oxygen
question: which primitive rings tile a closed polyhedron of a given face
census. The timed comparison is the how-to
[Cages and TRACE](../user/howto/cages-trace.md).

## The hydrogen-bond cage {#the-hydrogen-bond-cage}

A hydrogen bond is kept when the donor-acceptor oxygen distance is below
a cutoff and the angle at the donor oxygen, between the donated hydrogen
and the acceptor oxygen, is within the angle cutoff of a linear bond.
Rings are enumerated by depth-first search. A cup is a base ring plus
the lateral rings that share one edge with it. The cup closes when the
last lateral ring meets both of its neighbours. Complete and incomplete
cages are classified from those cups.

The TRACE program’s default cutoffs are 0.36 nm and 35°. The comparison
calls ClavisCage 0.3.18 at 0.35 nm and 35°. On an oxygen-only frame that
comparison places one hydrogen 0.96 Å from each oxygen along each of two
ice-rule bonds, then hands the waters to TRACE. d-SEAMS does not place
those hydrogens and does not call TRACE.

The three censuses in the comparison are $5^{12}$, $5^{12}6^{2}$ and
$5^{12}6^{4}$. On ice, which has no five-rings, both searches report
no cage of those three kinds. The counts are in the how-to above.

## A closed face list {#a-closed-face-list}

`seams_frame_signature` and `seams cages --signature` count a set of
primitive rings as one cage when three conditions hold. Every edge of
every face is shared by exactly two faces of the set. At least three
faces around each vertex form one cycle. The cell is a topological
sphere:

$$
V - E + F = 2.
$$

$F$ is the number of faces, $E$ the number of distinct edges, and
$V$ the number of distinct vertices. A ring whose minimum-image bond
shifts sum to a nonzero lattice vector winds through the periodic cell
and is dropped before this test. A cell thinner than twice the neighbour
cutoff is refused, because one pair can then meet through more than one
periodic image.

The default face-edge window is $[2.65, 3.15]$ in the coordinate units
of the file. `none` leaves the bound to the face census alone. On the
46-molecule sI cell, `--signature 512` reports 2 cages and 40 atoms with
the default window and with `none`.

The string `512` is twelve pentagons. `51262` is twelve pentagons and
two hexagons. `51264` is twelve pentagons and four hexagons. Joining
them with `+` prints one line per census. The call that takes the window
is `seams_frame_signature_edge`. The C API names are
`seams_signature_cages` and `seams_signature_cages_edge`.

[C++](../stable/cpp.md) documents `seams_frame_signature` and
`seams_frame_signature_edge`.
[C](../stable/c.md) documents `seams_signature_cages` and
`seams_signature_cages_edge`.


---

<!-- https://docs.dseams.info/explanation/trace-threads.md -->

# Signature-search thread controls {#signature-search-thread-controls}

The signature search reads one OpenMP width, and the neighbour list may
narrow it. The tables record that width on hydrate cells and on ice Ic.
`threads` is the width that was requested. On the signature and kernel
tables, `cores` is the number of CPUs the process was allowed. `n` is
the number of timed calls that were kept.

## How the rows were timed {#how-the-rows-were-timed}

The signature and kernel rows at width $n$ were run with this environment:

| variable | value |
| --- | --- |
| OMP_NUM_THREADS | n |
| OMP_DYNAMIC | FALSE |
| OMP_PROC_BIND | close |
| OMP_PLACES | cores |
| RAYON_NUM_THREADS | n |
| OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS, MKL_NUM_THREADS, NUMEXPR_NUM_THREADS | 1 |

The process was pinned to cpu 0 when $n = 1$, and to cpus 0 through
$n - 1$ otherwise. One warm-up was dropped. Eight timed calls remain.
The median of an even count is the mean of the two central samples. The
interquartile range is the type-7 upper quartile minus the lower one.

## The width the search reads {#the-width-the-search-reads}

`seams_set_num_threads` sets the OpenMP width later calls read, and the
linkcell width with it. Zero restores the width saved at first use.
`seams_get_num_threads` reports the width the next call will request.

`seams::teamFor` returns that OpenMP width. The atom count is not read.
`seams::TeamWidth` applies the width for the rest of the call and
restores the previous width afterwards. Bond order, published CHILL+,
the k-nearest list, the shell label and local $q_l$ use `TeamWidth`.
Those calls do not start a Rayon pool.

`seams::adoptThreads` calls `prepareCompute`, then `lc_set_threads` with
the OpenMP width. `prepareCompute` calls `omp_set_dynamic(0)` and leaves
`OMP_WAIT_POLICY` as the process started it. The environment above does
not set that variable. The linkcell workers sleep between searches.
Forcing a passive OpenMP wait on top of that sleep made the next region
late by tens of milliseconds, so the OpenMP team is left running.

`lc_set_threads` stores the width of later linkcell searches. A count
below one is stored as one thread, and one thread is a serial walk. A
width keeps its pool, and a later search at the same width reuses it.
A different width uses its own pool.

The C calls `seams_signature_cages` and `seams_signature_cages_edge`
enter through `seams::FairWidth`. When `SEAMS_FAIR_WIDTH` is unset, two
forks in a row that each take more than a millisecond halve the team,
down to a quarter of the requested width. A narrowed team tries twice
its width again at most once a second. `SEAMS_FAIR_WIDTH=0` keeps the
requested width. `seams_frame_signature` and `seams cages --signature`
do not enter through `FairWidth`.

[C](../stable/c.md) documents `seams_set_num_threads` and `seams_get_num_threads`.

## The neighbour list {#the-neighbour-list}

The timed hydrate sample is one cutoff list from `neighListLinkcell`,
one depth-6 primitive-ring network, and one search of $5^{12}$,
$5^{12}6^{2}$ and $5^{12}6^{4}$ together. Below 4096 molecules that
list caps the team at four and sets the OpenMP width to the cap. The
cap is left in place, so the ring search that follows runs at four
threads as well. A request for eight threads on sI $2\times2\times2$
(368 molecules), sI $4\times4\times4$ (2944) and sII $2\times2\times2$
(1088) therefore has the same width as the four-thread row, and the
medians sit together. At 4096 molecules and above the requested width
is kept.

Several threads in that list build an orthorhombic or triclinic cutoff
with the cell-list CSR. One thread uses linkcell’s buffered walk. If the
cell list cannot be built, the call uses that walk as well. Both builders
write the same sorted cutoff set, so the ring search does not depend on
which builder ran.

`seams cages --signature` on a cutoff graph calls `neighListO`, which
does not apply the 4096 cap. The C API builds an orthorhombic cutoff
with the cell list when every atom has the requested type, and uses
`neighListO` for a triclinic frame or a frame that mixes types.

`seams_frame_signature` on a single census uses the largest face as the
depth, so `512` alone is a depth-5 network. The timed sample above
searches all three censuses on one depth-6 network.

When the pairs come from a linkcell pair list, the rows stay on the
calling thread until the frame has at least 4096 atoms and the pair
list has at least $2^{20}$ pairs. Waking a team that slept through
the search costs more than writing those rows on the caller until the
list is that large. The several-thread cell-list path does not use
that placement.

| Signature cages on the sI and sII cells. threads is the width that was requested. n is the number of timed calls. The median of an even count is the mean of the two central samples. iqr_ms is the type-7 interquartile range. |
| --- |

## The ring update {#the-ring-update}

`sourceTeam` sizes the enumeration of changed ring sources, and the
carried update’s full pass. The calling thread does the work until
there are about 80 sources for every worker. `teamFor` is a different
rule: it is the requested width at every frame size.

On one thread the carried update copies the new rings and sorts them
directly, then merges the rings that stay with a direct walk. Several
threads sort indices, scan for rings that meet the changed set, and
merge the rings that are kept, using `teamFor`. Dropped ring buffers
are kept and reused by the next frame.

The cage index is merged from per-thread buckets in ring order.
Membership is the sorted atom ids of each face. The census at every
width is the one-thread census.

## Eight kernels {#eight-kernels}

Eight kernels are timed on ideal ice Ic at 4096, 32768, 110592 and
884736 molecules, each at 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads. They are primitive
rings, local and cutoff $q_4$ and $q_6$, CHILL+, the shell label,
and one carried hop update. The neighbour graph is built before the
timer starts. The rings kernel is `primitive::ringNetwork` on that
graph. Local $q_4$ and $q_6$ read the same graph. Cutoff $q_4$,
cutoff $q_6$ and published CHILL+ build their own cutoff list inside
the timed call. The hop kernel times the second update, after the first
update has filled the carried state. A repeat whose fingerprint differs
from the first call aborts the run. On 4096 molecules the kernels match
the one-thread result.

`seams_frame_rings` builds the cutoff list and then searches, so its
time is not this rings kernel.

| Eight kernels on ideal ice Ic, each at 1, 2, 4 and 8 threads. n is the number of timed calls. The median of an even count is the mean of the two central samples. iqr_ms is the type-7 interquartile range. |
| --- |

## The full cutoff ring call {#the-full-cutoff-ring-call}

The full call is the neighbour list, the index conversion and the
depth-6 search, timed together on ice Ic at 884736 molecules.
`cell-list` is the orthorhombic list inside that call. `linkcell` is
the buffered walk. `link`, `convert` and `search` are the three parts.
`total` is the whole call. This is not the rings kernel above.

Several threads take the half stencil one z layer at a time, in one
team. A layer stores a pair only on its own atoms. The partner row is
filled after the team has stopped, because a forward step in x reaches
back one z layer. An interior cell has no periodic image. Its thirteen
forward neighbours are plain index steps and the shift is zero, so
that cell skips the periodic-shift arithmetic. A boundary cell still
applies the shift. One thread uses the same half stencil without a
team. Below 2048 atoms the orthorhombic list runs on one thread and
then restores the caller’s width. Published CHILL+ and cutoff $q_6$
read this list. The one-thread and several-thread pair lists match.

The 4096-molecule cap and the $2^{20}$-pair row placement belong to
the signature search above. `teamFor` does not replace them.

| Ice Ic at 884736 molecules. cell-list is the orthorhombic cutoff list. linkcell is the buffered walk. total is the neighbour list, the index conversion and the depth-6 search. link, convert and search are those three parts. n is the number of timed calls. The median of an even count is the mean of the two central samples. iqr_ms is the type-7 interquartile range, filled on the total rows. |
| --- |

# Python Frame {#python-frame}

`dseams.userframe.read` in pydseamslib 2.14.0 returns a `Frame` over
`libseams_lang`. Install with `pip install 'pydseamslib==2.14.0'`.
`import pydseams` loads `pydseams.frame.Frame`.
That class has no `graph` argument on `chill_plus` and no `edge`
argument on `cages_by_signature`.
The calls below use `userframe`. The frame is
`input/traj/ice1h.lammpstrj`, 128 oxygens, and the line under each
call is the result on that cell.

## read {#read}

```python
>>> from dseams import userframe
>>> frame = userframe.read("input/traj/ice1h.lammpstrj", atom_type=1)
>>> frame.n_atoms
128
```

## steinhardt {#steinhardt}

```python
>>> from dseams import userframe
>>> frame = userframe.read("input/traj/ice1h.lammpstrj", atom_type=1)
>>> q = frame.steinhardt(6)
>>> sorted(q)
['ql', 'ql_bar']
>>> len(q["ql"])
128
>>> round(sum(q["ql"]) / len(q["ql"]), 6)
0.625855
```

## ring_census {#ring-census}

```python
>>> from dseams import userframe
>>> frame = userframe.read("input/traj/ice1h.lammpstrj", atom_type=1)
>>> frame.ring_census(6)
{6: 256}
```

## rdf_2d {#rdf-2d}

```python
>>> import tempfile
>>> from dseams import userframe
>>> frame = userframe.read("input/traj/ice1h.lammpstrj", atom_type=1)
>>> radius, values = frame.rdf_2d(tempfile.mkdtemp(), cutoff=6.0, binwidth=0.5)
>>> len(radius)
12
```

`len(radius)` is `int(cutoff / binwidth)`, here `int(6.0 / 0.5)`.
`values` is `g(r)` on those bin centers.

## monolayer_rings {#monolayer-rings}

```python
>>> import tempfile
>>> from dseams import userframe
>>> frame = userframe.read("input/traj/ice1h.lammpstrj", atom_type=1)
>>> sheet = frame.monolayer_rings(tempfile.mkdtemp(), sheet_area=1.0, max_depth=6)
>>> sheet[6]["count"]
256
```

## find_prisms {#find-prisms}

```python
>>> import tempfile
>>> from dseams import userframe
>>> frame = userframe.read("input/traj/ice1h.lammpstrj", atom_type=1)
>>> frame.find_prisms(output_dir=tempfile.mkdtemp(), max_depth=4)
[{'size': 3, 'perfect': 0, 'imperfect': 0}, {'size': 4, 'perfect': 0, 'imperfect': 0}]
```

`max_depth=4` asks for prism sizes 3 and 4.
This cell’s primitive rings are the 256 six-rings, so both sizes are empty and both counts stay 0.

## to_ase {#to-ase}
